5. Historical Data Collection

The technical documentation for the Sea Level indicator provides detailed discussion of how observational data were collected, including specific programs and the relative advantages of each method and how they complement each other. To summarize, sea level relative to the shore (“relative” sea level) is measured using tide gauges, which are mechanical measuring devices placed along the shore, while global mean sea level now comes from satellite measurement of sea surface heights (altimetry) relative to the center of the Earth.

Tide gauges devices measure the change in sea level relative to the land surface, which means the resulting data reflect both the change in absolute sea surface height and the change in local land levels. NOAA (2014) describes tide gauge data and how they were collected. Data collection methods are documented in a series of NOAA manuals and standards. EPA’s graph shows trends for a subset of stations along the ocean coasts that had sufficient data from 1960 to 2023.

Tide gauge data can be converted to absolute change through a series of adjustments as described in Section 6. This is how global mean sea level can be estimated prior to the onset of satellite measurement in 1979.

6. Indicator Derivation

Observed Data

NOAA processed all of the satellite measurements so they could be combined into a single time series. In doing so, NOAA limited its analysis to data between 66 degrees south and 66 degrees north, which covers a large majority of the Earth’s surface and represents the area with the most complete satellite coverage. The technical documentation for the Sea Level indicator provides citations and explains several adjustments and corrections that were made to ensure consistency across multiple satellite missions, adjust for air pressure differences and seasonal signals, and so on. NOAA reported data at approximately 10-day intervals, from which the project team calculated monthly and then annual averages.

CSIRO developed the long-term tide gauge reconstruction using a series of adjustments to convert relative tide gauge measurements into an absolute global mean sea level trend. Church and White (2011) describe the methods used, which include data screening; calibration with satellite altimeter data to establish patterns of spatial variability; and a correction for glacial isostatic adjustment, which represents the ongoing change in the size and shape of the ocean basins associated with changes in surface loading.

The graph shows annual change relative to the reconstruction’s 1880 starting point. The project team anchored the first year of the satellite time series (1993) to the corresponding data point in the reconstruction. The team has labeled the graph as “cumulative sea level change” for the sake of clarity.

For the map, NOAA used monthly sea level means to calculate a long-term annual rate of change for each station, which was determined by linear regression. Then, the annual rate of change was multiplied by the length of the analysis period to determine total change. This part of the analysis was limited to long-term tide gauges that met certain data availability criteria outlined in the technical documentation for the Sea Level indicator.

The inset plots on the map show average annual sea levels relative to the 1960s average for each station. The project team calculated annual values from monthly means for each year that had at least seven months of data.

Projections

The project team obtained source data from NOAA. NOAA’s scenarios present sea level change relative to the base year 2005, with data points at 2020, 2030, and every 10 years thereafter, ending in 2150. The two scenarios begin to diverge between 2020 and 2030. The project team converted from metric to English units to support accessibility to a wider U.S.-based audience.

7. Alignment

For the graphs, the project team aligned each projected time series to the observed satellite-based time series using the average of the years 2005 to 2020. Specifically, the team calculated the 2005–2020 average for the observed data, calculated the 2005–2020 average for the modeled data, calculated the difference between the two, and shifted all modeled values up or down by this amount. The satellite-based time series had already been chained to the long-term reconstruction at year 1993 as part of EPA’s Sea Level indicator. This chaining essentially results in the projections being shifted vertically on the graph, with no change to their shape or slope. The resulting graph now shows cumulative change relative to the start of the record in 1880.

For the map, the project team did not conduct any aligning steps as the maps shows the total change across years.

The results show good alignment. Thus, no other transformation was necessary.

8. Display

The interactive graph for this pairing shows the following elements:

  • Observed data from 1880 to 2023, encompassing CSIRO’s reconstruction for 1880–2013 and satellite altimetry for 1993–2023.
  • Projections for the two selected scenarios with data points at 2005 and 2020 (no divergence yet) and for 2020, 2030, and every 10 years thereafter until 2150. The graph displays straight lines to connect these decadal data points.
  • Shaded bands around the projections, representing the range of likely values as defined by NOAA from the 17th to 83rd

The interactive maps for this pairing show relative sea level change at specific locations, encompassing the following elements:

  • Observed data from EPA’s indicator, representing total change from 1960 to 2020.
  • Total change from 2020 to 2150 for each of the two chosen scenarios (intermediate-low, labeled “lower sea level rise,” and intermediate, labeled “higher sea level rise”).

9. Quality Assurance and Quality Control

Satellite data processing involves extensive quality assurance and quality control (QA/QC) protocols—for example, to check for instrumental drift by comparing with tide gauge data. The technical documentation for the Sea Level indicator provides citations that document these QA/QC procedures. Church and White (2011) and earlier publications cited therein describe steps that were taken to select the highest-quality sites and correct for various sources of potential error in tide gauge measurements used for the long-term reconstruction. Quality assurance and quality control procedures for U.S. tide gauge data are described in various publications available at NOAA’s CO-OPS Publications site. For each pairing, the project team conducted typical quality control steps including independently checking all aggregations, unit conversions, transformations, and other calculations.
